. At a time when quantum cryptography research was focussing on the symmetric scenarios of secure-two-party computation and hitting the no-go result for unconditionally secure bit commitment, I was the first to shift the focus on the asymmetric scenario of “blind quantum computing”. My protocol offers an efficient, quantum alternative to the later discovered classical homomorphic encryption scheme. The topic has become a full-blown research topic and enjoyed experimental demonstration.
A structure theorem for discrete-time discrete-space quantum theory

. We proved a general, mathematical physics theorem applicable to any quantum evolutions in discrete space, showing that these can always be represented by a finite-depth circuit of local quantum gates.
Proof of the Church-Turing thesis from quantum, physical hypotheses

. Robin Gandy (Alan Turing’s PhD student) has proved the Church-Turing thesis from physical hypotheses. Indeed, a number of natural assumptions (homogeneity, causality, bounded density) entail that the evolution of any physical system must be computable. Based on the previous structure theorem, we generalised Gandy’s theorem to the quantum setting.

. Focussing on the case where the discrete space is a grid leads to quantum cellular automata (QCA). We constructed minimal examples of intrinsically universal QCA, which are capable of simulating all other QCA in a spacetime-preserving manner, thereby contributing to export the Computer Science notion of universality, to the realm of Physics, including via popular science.

. Focussing on the one-particle case of QCA leads to quantum walks (QW). We proved in full rigour, using numerical analysis methods, that some QW converge towards the dynamics of real-life particles, such as the propagation of the electron— thereby providing very simple, algorithmic explanations of their behaviours, as well as quantum simulation algorithms for them. We showed that, surprisingly, QW can even simulate particles in curved spacetime, in spite of their fixed background grid.
Quantum cellular automata for simulating particles

. Back to the many-particle case, we provided the first QCA model for real-life interacting particles, namely electrons and photons, a.k.a 3+1 quantum electrodynamics. We motivated our construction by proposing a discrete version of a fundamental symmetry of Physics, namely gauge symmetry, which turns out to be reminiscent of fault-tolerance in Computer Science. This opens the way for natively discrete formulations of quantum field theories, otherwise renowned for their ill-definedness.

. We generalised the fundamental theorems of Cellular Automata theory, namely their topological characterization as continuous functions, and consequences, to causal dynamics over arbitrary bounded-degree time-varying graphs. We also generalised the block-decomposition theorem from Reversible Cellular Automata to Reversible Causal Graph Dynamics, and dealt with the intricate question whether reversibility forbids the local creation/destruction of nodes.

. Extending the structure theorem to the quantum setting was particularly challenging, because it is no longer clear whom is next to whom, when two nodes may be in a quantum superposition of being connected, or not. We therefore had to generalise the standard concepts of locality, causality, and reduced density matrix to these quantum superpositions of topologies. We did so in a very satisfactory manner: all of the logical relations between these concepts are preserved.
Linear-algebraic λ-calculus and vectorial type systems

. Whilst partly unexplained, it is clear that the algorithmic speed-up of Quantum Computation arises by tapping into the parallelism granted by the superposition principle. The idea of a vector space of computations arises quite naturally in this context. We designed the Linear-algebraic λ-calculus, merging higher-order computation, be it terminating or not, in its simplest and most general form (namely the untyped λ-calculus) with linear algebra in its simplest and most general form also (the oriented axioms of vector spaces we obtained beforehand), and proved its confluence.
